title: Compound Risk and Centralized Desalination: Multi‐Hazard Threats to Water Security
content:
Abstract

Water security research has long acknowledged that engineered water systems face concurrent threat pathways, yet risk assessment practice remains predominantly single-hazard. For desalination-dependent systems—nowhere more than in the Gulf—this simplification is a structural failure. We argue in this Commentary that centralized desalination systems concentrate three mutually reinforcing sources of compound vulnerability: structural compounding—near-total dependence on desalinated water, extreme concentration of production in a small number of very large facilities, and tight physical coupling of water production to power generation; multi-hazard concurrence—simultaneous exposure to kinetic attack, energy disruption, cyber intrusion, and environmental contamination, superimposed on chronic drought and groundwater depletion; and non-linear interaction effects, through which concurrent stressors amplify one another. The strikes on power and desalination-related infrastructure across the Gulf in March 2026—in a region producing on the order of 40 per cent of the world's desalinated water—illustrate how these dimensions combine in practice. We map the compound exposure pathways of desalination infrastructure, identify the structural mismatch between centralized desalination architectures and the international humanitarian law framework nominally protecting them, and propose three actionable interventions: mandatory compound vulnerability assessment as a condition of international financing, a structural shift toward distributed solar-driven reverse-osmosis architectures, and a dedicated international instrument for the categorical protection of large-scale desalination infrastructure as civilian infrastructure indispensable to survival.
